A teenage boy confronts the challenges of identifying with the hyper-sexuality and rigid masculinity that surrounds him during a weekend trip to meet his estranged father's new girlfriend. 'Melograno' is a compelling exploration of the inner turmoil a young teenage boy faces during a weekend trip to meet his estranged father's new girlfriend. Against the picturesque backdrop of the Australian countryside, the film delves into the pervasive issues of misogyny and toxic masculinity, both deeply rooted in society. As the story unfolds, we follow the young protagonist's journey, a poignant coming-of-age tale that strikes a chord with anyone who has ever felt pressured to conform to gender norms and expectations. In his case, these expectations revolve around embracing a hyper-sexualized and performative version of masculinity passed down through generations. The heart of the film lies in the young boy's internal struggle. He grapples with a conflicting desire to forge his identity and assert his individuality while facing the overwhelming weight of societal conformity. 'Melograno' is a window into the emotional complexities of this journey, painting a vivid portrait of his inner conflict. The film's narrative serves as a catalyst for introspection and conversation. It challenges viewers to reflect on these pressing issues, exploring the intricate web of gender dynamics and toxic masculinity. It's a stark reminder of the need to address these topics, prompt societal attitudes change, and move towards a more inclusive and understanding world. Youth, and even teenage for that matter, are rather umbrella terms; great for convenience, but they come up rather short in encompassing the many explosions of development that make up these years. Noah Stratton-Twine’s sublime drama _Young, Young Men_ examines with finesse and refreshing empathy that effervescent period of high school, putting the focus on two teenage boys, in a way that teenage boys have rarely been seen or understood.
Stream Indie Films
The film opens on the first day of summer vacation, ’09. Luke (John Worthy) and Charlie (Ned Wakeley) have just received their results, one barely perturbed by it, and the other barely hiding his perturbation. This suppressed regret and denial of embarrassment is a persistent characteristic of Charlie. The film reveals the personalities of its two characters through stray dialogues and little gestures in the actors’ performances. As reserved as Charlie is, Luke is openly sensitive and even somewhat childlike. Their friendship is one of open solidarity and sincere affection.
As the camera lingers upon each face, it is not hard to see how respectfully human Stratton-Twine has made his characters. The camera, and by extension the audience, really sees these two teenage boys who hang out, out of genuine affection and friendship, and not convenience born of familiarity born of circumstance, endearing them to the audience almost immediately.
Stream Indie Films
Cinematography and setting echoes the premise and feel of the film. Luke and Charlie walk through woods, by ponds, coming finally to rest in a big field, against the backdrop of a brilliant sunset. Whether it is the handheld camera or the quick cuts, it gets to the essence of teenhood, of both languid and fun afternoons, sometimes contentedly aimless, sometimes pushing for wider horizons. Frankly, _Young, Young Men_ is beautiful enough to make even clumsy attempts at getting laid have touching emotion.

# Young, Young Men: Teen Boys Have Rarely Been Seen As Well
### Indie Shorts Mag Rating
To complement this, music is painfully beautiful, the very opening sequence saying everything before the visuals have even begun rolling. It is anticipatory, not only buzzing with excitement at things to come within the scope of the film, but also an electric, bittersweet cry out to all the changes about to happen.
Stream Indie Films
The film ends on a poignant sunset, their separation looming in the air.
Charlie and Luke, these two darling young men, fledgeling adults, so full of endearing sulkiness that they are unforgettable, are impossible to not love. _Young, Young Men_ is that. Unforgettable and entirely beautiful.

# Young, Young Men: Teen Boys Have Rarely Been Seen As Well
### Indie Shorts Mag Rating

Summarize with ChatGPT Summarize with Grok Summarize with Perplexity
Youth, and even teenage for that matter, are rather umbrella terms; great for convenience, but they come up rather short in encompassing the many explosions of development that make up these years. Noah Stratton-Twine’s sublime drama _Young, Young Men_ examines with finesse and refreshing empathy that effervescent period of high school, putting the focus on two teenage boys, in a way that teenage boys have rarely been seen or understood.
Stream Indie Films
The film opens on the first day of summer vacation, ’09. Luke (John Worthy) and Charlie (Ned Wakeley) have just received their results, one barely perturbed by it, and the other barely hiding his perturbation. This suppressed regret and denial of embarrassment is a persistent characteristic of Charlie. The film reveals the personalities of its two characters through stray dialogues and little gestures in the actors’ performances. As reserved as Charlie is, Luke is openly sensitive and even somewhat childlike. Their friendship is one of open solidarity and sincere affection.
As the camera lingers upon each face, it is not hard to see how respectfully human Stratton-Twine has made his characters. The camera, and by extension the audience, really sees these two teenage boys who hang out, out of genuine affection and friendship, and not convenience born of familiarity born of circumstance, endearing them to the audience almost immediately.
Stream Indie Films
Cinematography and setting echoes the premise and feel of the film. Luke and Charlie walk through woods, by ponds, coming finally to rest in a big field, against the backdrop of a brilliant sunset. Whether it is the handheld camera or the quick cuts, it gets to the essence of teenhood, of both languid and fun afternoons, sometimes contentedly aimless, sometimes pushing for wider horizons. Frankly, _Young, Young Men_ is beautiful enough to make even clumsy attempts at getting laid have touching emotion.

# Young, Young Men: Teen Boys Have Rarely Been Seen As Well
### Indie Shorts Mag Rating
To complement this, music is painfully beautiful, the very opening sequence saying everything before the visuals have even begun rolling. It is anticipatory, not only buzzing with excitement at things to come within the scope of the film, but also an electric, bittersweet cry out to all the changes about to happen.
Stream Indie Films
The film ends on a poignant sunset, their separation looming in the air.
Charlie and Luke, these two darling young men, fledgeling adults, so full of endearing sulkiness that they are unforgettable, are impossible to not love. _Young, Young Men_ is that. Unforgettable and entirely beautiful.

**Lew:** I don't know when it happened in the intervening period, but there was more of—a thicker layer of political appointees, mid-level political appointees, doing some of the most critical analysis and preparation. I think, in some ways, it was a response to the fact that there'd been some diminution of that skill level in the career staff. I think it may have, in part, been that some of my predecessors didn't have as much confidence in the career staff. I don't know how much—I know that I inherited a career staff that didn't have as sharp an edge as the one I left behind, but there were a lot of very good people there. And I made it my business when I came back to bring talent from the career staff into that process in a way that I think was important to the organization, to show that I'm not going to do it in a way that dismisses the career staff from the most sensitive and important analysis.
**Lew:** I mean, OMB's real strength is its ability to reach across the government to both see and assemble data, to create options where others don't have options. When I worked for Speaker O'Neill, I remember walking into negotiations with Dave Stockman, and I'd have a folder, and he'd have a notebook. You know, mine would be an inch thick and his would be six inches thick. He always had something at his fingertips that we could get by going to the committee staff, going to CBO, but we didn't have it at the—we hadn't run twenty-five scenarios of what to do if the other side did x, y, or z. And when I was at OMB the first time, in the Clinton administration, I very much used that resource to give me the ability to advance the president's agenda, and I did the same thing in the Obama administration. So I didn't find any difference in terms of OMB being able to do that for me.

**Lew:** Where I think there was a bit of a difference is, OMB's system was an almost archaic—is an almost archaic system of data processing, and it needed to make a transition to be able to do things in real time, on spreadsheets, with the kind of alacrity that a whiz kid with a computer in 2008 could do. It wouldn't be a hundred percent perfect, because it would miss some of the interactions that the big mainframe could pick up, but it was close enough to keep the process moving and then check it. I think that had I stayed at OMB longer, that was the top of my priority list, to make sure I left OMB with the capacity to play that kind of role with new technology to be as agile as I thought it needed to be.
**Lew:** I'm going to skip over the appropriations negotiations in 2011 to the grand bargain. When we went into the grand-bargain negotiations, the OMB staff was able to do for me everything that it was able to do in the 1990s. I remember there was a process that got set up that was cochaired by Vice President Biden and House majority leader Eric Cantor. You know, strange bedfellows, but they actually developed a warmth and friendship, as I did with Eric Cantor. President Obama never did with Eric Cantor. They were always very much bristly with each other. But the way I developed that relationship with Eric Cantor was—the way the Biden/Cantor process worked was, I was going to brief the group, as OMB director, on all the options for ways to fill a bucket of what we called other mandatory savings: not Medicare, not Medicaid, not Social Security; everything else. And we went through hundreds of items. I think Cantor saw pretty quickly that I was straight. I mean, he had smart people working for him; they never had to say, “That's not correct.” And he developed a confidence that whatever my point of view was, I was going to lay the facts out honestly. Well, it's a lot of power when OMB gives you the ability to play that role in a room.

**Lew:** We actually assembled a list of several hundred billion dollars of things that Cantor and Biden could agree on, and there was no grand bargain, but as you go forward and look at all the little deals that got done after the budget crisis, and when there had to be a relief from the sequestration that was ultimately enacted as part of the budget—what was the name of it? The Budget Enforcement Act? I'm forgetting now what the name of the 2011 sequestration bill was. I should remember it, but I blocked it.
**Lew:**Budget Control Act, the BCA, that's right. The Budget Enforcement Act was Andrews Air Force Base. All of the subsequent deals that, when he was Budget Committee chairman, Paul Ryan and Senator Patty Murray were able to agree to all came out of what we had cobbled together in the months sitting in those rooms together. So it was kind of a glimmer that OMB still had the ability to—I mean, I was the mouthpiece. It's not like I had prior knowledge of more than half of the programs. OMB gives you the ability to speak knowledgeably about things that are new to you. It gives you the ability to sit in a room where you know more than anyone else in the room, even though you didn't know anything about it the day before. That's what was in the notebooks that Dave Stockman had, and in my experience OMB still left me able to do that, even with some loss of edge on some of the—
**Lew:** I mean, the kind of power center, intellectual power center, of OMB was the division that had multiple responsibilities. One was doing cross-government exercises, called BDRs—I struggle to remember what it stands for [budget data requests] —and the other was budget concepts. And the budget-concepts people came through, because the bill that was drafted that put sequestration in place, the Budget Control Act, was written by two guys at my conference table in, basically longhand, because they knew how to do it. They knew how to take the guidance and convert it into a law in unbelievably rapid time, to avoid having a default at the end of that crisis. So I don't want to suggest that OMB had lost its kind of core abilities; there just was a need for a mainframe culture to adapt to the fast pace of policy development in a new world of laptop modelling.

**Lew:** There wasn't great morale at OMB when I got there. I think there was a sense that they were being kind of passed over in some of the first two years of the Obama administration, and my mission, my assignment from President Obama, was: “I know that when you walk in the door, your walking in the door is going to solve that, because people have told me what the morale is going to be when you walk in the door.” He said, “That's one of the reasons I need you to do this.” And I think it worked, in a sense, because I was like one of them. I was the closest thing to being one of them as a political appointee could be. They have to dump on the political people, because it's part of the culture. There's the gray building and there's the red building. The career people work in the red building; the political people work in the gray building. There's always going to be the gray and the red cultures, but I came as close to being accepted by the red-building culture as somebody who lived in the gray building could get, because I'd been there six years, and they knew that I cared deeply about what they did.
**Lew:** When I came back I don't think they knew how hard they were going to work for the next year [laughs] , because no one could imagine going from crisis to crisis, through holidays, literally through every holiday. I remember on Memorial Day and July Fourth being in the kind of peak of battle mode and getting an hour off for the fireworks. [Laughter]
**Q:** So you feel like you left OMB better than—

**Lew:** And the president called me— [laughs] In the eight years of the Obama administration I think I went home sick one day, and it was the day I went home sick, so I was at home with a fever, and the president calls and says, “Jack, I hear you went home sick. I hope you're feeling better, but I want to tell you something: tomorrow Bill Daley is going to be resigning, and I would like to announce you as my new chief of staff. And I said, “Mr. President, I'm honored that you feel that way.” And I said to him, “It's not a job I ever particularly aspired to, but I respect greatly the importance of it. It is the world's biggest pressure cooker, and it's not a decision I can make on my own, particularly not lying in bed with a fever. I've got to call Ruth and talk to my wife. It's a family decision. Let me do that and call you back.”
**Lew:** Why do you want me to be your chief of staff in 2012? You're going to be running for reelection, and it is the most political year of any eight-year presidency, and that's not what I do. I'm not going to be able to help you figure out what you need to do in Pennsylvania or Wisconsin. There are other people who do that for a living.” He said, “That's true, and I've got those people, but they also tell me, and I know they're right, that I'm going to be out there running for president four days a week, and I need a chief of staff who can be my alter ego, who can run this White House and this administration as if I was there, and I trust you to do that.”
**Lew:** So it was a little overwhelming, but—and, as I say, my wife is a true patriot. Her response was, “You can't say no, but you'd better make it a promise to me that you're going to go to the gym every day, because I need you at the end of this.” [Laughter]
**Q:** Did you keep that promise?

**Lew:** I did. Not every day, but certainly I started swimming four or five days a week, and I still do today, and now she thinks I'm a bit of a nut about being disciplined about it. “Actually,” I said, “you're the one who got me started.” [Laughter]
**Q:** When you first stepped into that role, were there things about the process or the structure that you changed?
**Lew:** So, you know, he made the commitment to me that there would be no decision of any consequence that I wasn't fully aware of and have a chance to advise on. There'd be no process that I didn't see, and I'd get to run the White House the way I would. He said, “I know how you deal with people. I know how you bring people together and consult people. You do it the way I would do it. I'm totally comfortable letting you kind of—” There were a few people—he didn't want to have turnover that was unnecessary, and I'm not a “new brush sweeps clean” kind of guy. Some people are. They come in and they say, “I want all my own people.” But when I went to OMB, I kept people who were there before me. When I later went to Treasury, I kept people who were there before me. I always tried to have continuity and have a transition happen gradually, not just say, “Well, I'm the new boss. Thanks for your service.” So that wasn't a big deal to me.

**Lew:** I mean, the challenge in an election year is, there's less of the president's time, so the chief of staff is much more the last stop than in a normal year. When the president is down the hall and if you need to you walk down, you call a meeting—we didn't have that much of his time as we did before or after. So the challenge was to make sure that in all of the decisions we were making, he knew what the views, if they were differing views, were, and could decide if he needed to fit time in to hear it directly. And I needed people to know that their views were going to him, because the whole system would have broken down. I mean, Bill Daley, who preceded me, had a bit of a reputation for being secretive. I think I have the reputation of being a little bit more transparent, so that helps. But it was a dicey situation, because people were used to being able to sit around a table, or in his office around the couches, and kind of offer their own two cents, and that wasn't going to be on every issue, certainly not with the frequency that it otherwise would be.
**Lew:** I pulled the senior staff together in my office, and I made clear I wasn't a “new brush sweeps clean” kind of guy; I wasn't looking to push people out of their roles, and everybody knew me, and I knew everybody, so this doesn't have to be a violent transition. And I said, “Look, I'll make you a commitment: if there's ever disagreements around this table, my chief of staff table, he will know the different points of view, whether he's here and can hear it or not. But you need to make a commitment to me that if you have a differing view, we hear it at this table. There can't be things going to him that don't come through this process. It won't work that way.” My last day as chief of staff, he said to me, “I think I kept my promise. I don't think there was a single decision that didn't go through your office, of any consequence.” It's not that he didn't have social conversations with people. It's not—but he would send everybody back.

**Lew:** There were times when I had to call people on it, where particularly people who had the ability to reach him directly sometimes wanted to keep their own counsel at the table, and on the toughest issue I would go around the room and I'd say, “If I didn't hear from you here, there's no reclama. You don't get to go and make another case. So do you have a view? Do you have a view? Do you have a view?” I just went around the table, and I—and there were some pretty big decisions, like DACA, the Deferred Action for Children, which, we're sitting here on a day when the Supreme Court is hearing oral arguments on whether or not the decision to reverse it was lawful, it was a hard issue to work through, probably the biggest policy issue of my year as chief of staff. We weren't making that much new policy in an election year, but DACA was a big deal.
**Lew:** In the first two years, first three years, the combination of legal analysis and agency views produced a null set in terms of what you could do administratively. The president asked Kathy Ruemmler, who was White House counsel, and me, as chief of staff, to—if we could—not even look at the work that was done before us. He said, “I want you to start from scratch. Things don't always stay the same. Some options change. I want to do something on this.” And it wasn't like I didn't agree with him. One of the issues I've been passionate about in my career has been immigration. I worked on immigration reform in the '80s. I worked on it in the '90s. So it's not like I was in any way disagreeing with him, but it was a pretty daunting assignment when you knew the White House counsel and the Department of Homeland Security and the Justice Department had done this and come up with nothing.

**Lew:** So Kathy and I started from scratch, and we worked with the policy teams. We worked with the Department of Homeland Security. And we said, “What if we take a whole different approach, and we just look at what can you do through prosecutorial discretion?” Because you have broad latitude on prosecutorial discretion. Not every crime is prosecuted equally. You don't have to put resources into everything equally. You can't say it's legal, but can you create a space where you can give people at least some temporary protection so that they can get on with their lives? And the interesting thing is, there was a lawful way—in my view; the Supreme Court will maybe decide—to do that. And let's remember the stakes: we didn't know if it was five hundred thousand or a million children who would be affected. These are children who came to this country, grew up here. They didn't cross the border of their own volition; they might have been babies. They went to school here. They served in our armed forces. They were going to our colleges. They were people who, in every way, thought of themselves as Americans, but they had this ambiguity about their status that was a cloud over their ability to get on with their lives. And in order for an approach that involves the kind of discretion that we're talking about here to work, you need the cooperation of the agency that's the enforcement agency. You can't make it happen if there's not a buy-in.

**Lew:** And, you know, he never said another nasty word about me after that, but he didn't vote for me, because he'd already said he wasn't going to vote for me. I think he respected that—I mean, I told him, “I didn't grow up rich like you think I did. I grew up with holes in my shoes. I've worked every day since I was seventeen years old and had, early in my life, responsibilities to support disabled relatives. So don't tell me I don't understand how people who are struggling live. Just don't tell me that. Yes, you didn't like that I worked at Citi for a couple years. I get it. But that doesn't mean you know who I am.”
**Lew:** The exchange at the hearing that, I think, cemented for him that I was “one of them” was over the causes of the financial crisis, where he was just wrong. He said the repeal of Glass-Steagall caused the financial crisis. I said, “Senator, we can debate what the cause of the financial crisis was, but the institutions that failed, that triggered the financial crisis, were doing the same thing they did before Glass-Steagall was repealed. They lived on one side of the line. Lehman [Brothers] was Lehman; Bear [Stearns] was Bear.” And I said there may have been a lot of things that should have been done differently, but it's just not accurate that it was the repeal of Glass-Steagall that caused it, and he took from that exchange that I was being an apologist for the banks. So that was his view of me. It never got any more sophisticated than that. We never really dealt with each other very much after that.
**Q:** You've said before that you spent some time at the Treasury winding down TARP.
**Lew:** Yeah.
**Q:** What did you mean by that?

**Lew:** I got to Treasury in 2013. We were out of the recession. Financial institutions were anxious to pay back TARP and to get out from under quasi-receivership. Institutions like General Motors that had to come and have me approve their compensation plans were anxious to get back to business as usual where they got to do what they wanted on their compensation plans. So we had to have an orderly process of exiting from TARP. It was in no one's interest to extend it. And the question was, do you try to market-time to sell GM stock when the price is good. We did what I would advise somebody to do in the private sector: you have a plan, you execute it, and you don't try to market-time it, and you get out in an orderly way, and on average you'll do okay. I mean, you could easily make a big mistake doing it the other way.
**Lew:** We ended up recovering more than was spent on TARP in repayment, and there were some assets that were valued higher, others that were valued lower, but in the end, if you just look at TARP as, “Did the taxpayers pay for the bailout?” No. It was repaid. Now, that's only half the equation. You look at the damage done to the economy vast damage done to the economy. And how do you measure that? How do you repay for that? I think the political anger that we're still living with is flowing from the fact that it didn't really matter to people that TARP was repaid; it was that the people who caused the crisis got back on their feet, and we didn't. It was that the people who did something wrong didn't go to jail. It was what Tim used to call the desire for Old Testament judgment. It's not my kind of language, but he used to call it that.

**Lew:** The irony is, when I was at OMB, money was not the issue in looking for criminal violations. When I was chief of staff, money was not the issue, and when I was at Treasury money was—the Justice Department had as much resources as it needed. They never found the criminal case to prosecute. And I'm proud to say that our view of the executive branch was you only prosecute when there are crimes, not to make a political statement. You don't put somebody's head on a pike because you want to win a political battle. And I would say of the issues that the president was frustrated over, he saw the schism in the country that was coming from the desire for a greater sense that people who did something wrong needed to pay for it. And it wasn't even in terms of his own politics. I mean, I don't think he thought it was going to be an issue for his politics. He was worried that it was going to undermine confidence in institutions the way it turns out to have. I think had it been like Enron, where there was somebody who could be indicted and pay a price, it probably would have been better for the country.
**Lew:** On the other hand, I'm proud that we didn't just try to indict somebody to make that point, even if we thought it was the right thing in terms of the kind of well-being of democracy. I mean, obviously I'm sitting here in 2020 saying that at a time where there's all kinds of questions about how the lines between Justice Department decision-making and political calculation are very problematic. I remember sitting in a car with the president when the head of state of a very close ally called and said if a certain prosecution goes forward, it could cause a national crisis, economic crisis, damage our relations. And the president said, “Look, our countries are dear friends. We're dear friends. I don't tell the Justice Department what crimes to go after, or what not to go after.”
**Lew:** So this was in a class of frustrating outcomes where we're now in over ten years of uninterrupted economic growth, uninterrupted job growth, people's 401[k]s, IRAs [individual retirement accounts] more than fully restored. There's a lot of ways you can say the recovery was slow but successful. You look at the political and social landscape, and the damage is deep, and I worry about that.

**Q:** We'd like to pivot to some of the foreign policy issues you confronted at Treasury, the first of which being China. In 2006, the Bush administration had created the Strategic Economic Dialogue [SED] . In 2009 the Obama administration stood up the Strategic and Economic Dialogue. Was there significance in that name change?
**Lew:** Well, I must say there is significance. I didn't understand at the time, sitting in the State Department, how symbolic, how much energy would go into thinking about the meaning of it. It seemed obvious to us at the State Department in the first year that the issues between the US and China surely were economic, but they were as much strategic, and we didn't have great mil-mil dialogues between our military and the PLA [People's Liberation Army] . We didn't have the level of connectivity between the State Department and State Council and Foreign Ministry that we should have on hard issues, new issues like cyber, and were not, strictly speaking, economic. I mean, they had economic and strategic components. So the idea was to broaden it, and make it include both, and have two tracks, and have the relationships on both sides evolve.
**Lew:** Treasury wasn't so crazy about the idea, and it's interesting: in the years since, my good friend Hank Paulson continues to talk about the SED, and thinks it was a mistake to expand it to include the strategic issues. And there was some jockeying at the beginning of how many State Department people would be there, and [laughs] it had sometimes comical but classic Washington turf aspects to it. I actually think the way it went forward was quite good. I played a small role in the first one where I was the counterpart on development issues to the Chinese representatives. When I was at OMB and chief of staff, I came in on an issue here, an issue there, but as Treasury secretary I owned the Strategic and Economic Dialogue. And I went into it with some background, but it was the case where I had to get to know a whole new cast of characters. My counterpart was somebody that I met for the first time when we were both named special representative of our respective leaders, and I ended up quickly forging a very good working relationship with him.

**Lew:** Now, some of us may have thought it would have still made sense, while others were happy to leave it behind. That's a separate issue. It's not like everyone, even in the administration, was of one view. Even individuals had—I know I had competing views in my own mind. I think the president had some competing views in his own mind. But once you know you can't do it, you don't spend a lot of your energy trying.
**Q:** I hadn't known much of that. Thanks. Thanks for that. I mentioned I wanted to return to the international global community—and I do—to ask you about Cuba, which I haven't yet had a chance to ask you about over our sessions. And maybe I'll start here. In September of 2015, the Treasury Department joined the Department of Commerce in taking measures to try to normalize relations between the US and Cuba. At the time, you said that action “underscored the administration's commitment to promote successful change for the Cuban people.” What were the aims of the actions the administration took, especially at Treasury, towards Cuba in 2015?
**Lew:** So, there had been a fifty-year economic embargo on Cuba that included all kinds of sanctions that were Treasury-enforced sanctions on dealing with Cuba. The sequence of events—it didn't originate at Treasury. There was a very secret and quiet negotiation driven out of the National Security Council. Ben Rhodes was very much a leader in the effort to work through a way of dealing with Cuba directly on these issues.
**Lew:** When Treasury, which was one of the—I think we were the first non–White House agency that was read into the conversation. They may have been surprised that we were enthusiastically for it, because the Cuba sanctions were viewed as entirely ineffective, harming US economically, and probably setting back the efforts of making things better in Cuba. So there was not a feeling in Treasury that it was a well-designed—even though it was fifty years old—that it was a well-designed, effective set of tools. The political issues surrounding relaxing sanctions on Cuba were much more difficult than the policy and intellectual issues behind the sanctions structure.

**Lew:** Where we got involved was lifting specific sanctions. And I remember going through them with our team from the office at Treasury that deals with sanctions, OFAC, item by item. We were careful to try and do the things that would most encourage people-to-people contact, which had, for a long time, been seen as increasing the likelihood of change in Cuba; helping the Cuban people, who were suffering under economic sanctions that weren't leading to the political aim of sanctions, changing the sovereign policy. The government was not responding to the fact that for decades, it was hurting the Cuban economy. But the Cuban people were hurting.
**Lew:** But we didn't want to be funding the government. We didn't want to give the government the ability to commandeer the benefits of all of the relaxation. And there's no perfect solution, because governments have taxing authority, and it's hard to say that if business increases, and government revenues go in on a normal basis, then you're not helping the larger government. But we tried to avoid the things that would provide lopsided benefit to the government, as opposed to the rank and file. And some of the issues got to things like baseball players [laughs] and things that—where it was very easy to see how it would not be the intended beneficiaries who got the benefit.
**Q:** You, of course, served in the Department of State during the president's first year in office. In 2016, you talked to the reporters a bit about sanctions in a few interviews, and you noted that they were a powerful tool but they shouldn't be used “frivolously.” You also said that policy makers should be as thoughtful about the use of sanctions as they are about the use of military force. I wanted to ask: In that time between 2009 and 2016, how had your view of sanctions evolved, and had your views of sanctions been shaped by your involvement in modifying sanctions against Cuba?

**Lew:** You know, my knowledge of sanctions policy grew quite dramatically in the period from '09 to '17. I worked on some of these sanctions issues from the State Department. And I'll give you an example. This wasn't a Treasury authority, but it's very much the same kind of calculus. I was at the State Department when the Iran sanctions on oil were being negotiated with Congress. This was '09. Congress, including some members of Congress I was very close to, wanted to take the toughest position they could possibly take. And we were pretty confident that if that was the outcome, we wouldn't get the international cooperation that you would need for a sanctions regime to be effective, for countries like Russia and China to participate and not circumvent the sanctions.
**Lew:** We ended up negotiating with Congress to get the flexibility so that you could have, in terms of oil sanctions, variable degrees of reduction, country by country. So if you have a country whose economy would grind to a halt if you shut off all oil imports, they wouldn't have to reduce consumption as much as a country that had very little Iranian oil. And we ended up coming out of it with the lineup that led to the P5+1 talks with Iran and produced the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. China and Russia were very much part of that process. They wouldn't have been if we had done the toughest thing.
**Lew:** So in designing the most effective sanctions regime—and in the things that I said in 2016, I very much spoke to this issue—the purpose of a sanction regime is not just to cause pain to another country; it's to change the policy of another sovereign, to bring the vectors of pressure to bear to accomplish a diplomatic goal. And we did that with Iran by doing it in a way that some might have said wasn't as tough, because it's not always as obvious as, the more severe sanction is going to be more effective.

**Lew:** Something that I learned from '09 through the time I was at Treasury was, war weariness was putting more and more pressure on economic sanctions, because the credibility of threatening to use US force was just in a different place after Iraq and Afghanistan than before. There was just a general sense that the stakes of the US getting involved militarily on the ground had changed. They were not zero, but the bar was higher. The number of circumstances that the US wants to project its influence in doesn't go down when your likelihood or willingness to use force is somewhat lower. Economic tools were a way to use our influence to try to achieve change.
**Lew:** I actually don't think that's a bad thing. I think if you can achieve your change with economic tools instead of putting lives on the line, the world is a better place. But it means you can't do it frivolously, and you can't do it symbolically; because you use those economic tools, you're hurting people. I mean, see Cuba. The Cuban people were poor. The people of North Korea are more poor. The people of Iran were more poor. If it's accomplishing a purpose, you do it in a way that you try to make clear that you don't want to hurt people, but you want the government to change its policy. In a situation where there's no diplomatic strategy that can work, where all it is is hurting people, I think you have to be careful. It may make you feel like you've done something that's moral, but if you actually take it apart, you've caused collateral damage to people who have no ability to change the policy and done nothing to affect the policy-making calculus.
**Lew:** The remarks I gave were actually that it's important to strengthen the tools, not to say don't use them, and, candidly, to make sure that they're there twenty-five, thirty years from now, and they don't get overused and create a flight from the dollar to get away from US pressure—which is not anytime soon, but it's a risk you have to worry about.

**Lew:** I don't know when it happened in the intervening period, but there was more of—a thicker layer of political appointees, mid-level political appointees, doing some of the most critical analysis and preparation. I think, in some ways, it was a response to the fact that there'd been some diminution of that skill level in the career staff. I think it may have, in part, been that some of my predecessors didn't have as much confidence in the career staff. I don't know how much—I know that I inherited a career staff that didn't have as sharp an edge as the one I left behind, but there were a lot of very good people there. And I made it my business when I came back to bring talent from the career staff into that process in a way that I think was important to the organization, to show that I'm not going to do it in a way that dismisses the career staff from the most sensitive and important analysis.
**Lew:** I mean, OMB's real strength is its ability to reach across the government to both see and assemble data, to create options where others don't have options. When I worked for Speaker O'Neill, I remember walking into negotiations with Dave Stockman, and I'd have a folder, and he'd have a notebook. You know, mine would be an inch thick and his would be six inches thick. He always had something at his fingertips that we could get by going to the committee staff, going to CBO, but we didn't have it at the—we hadn't run twenty-five scenarios of what to do if the other side did x, y, or z. And when I was at OMB the first time, in the Clinton administration, I very much used that resource to give me the ability to advance the president's agenda, and I did the same thing in the Obama administration. So I didn't find any difference in terms of OMB being able to do that for me.
texts.60:
**Lew:** Where I think there was a bit of a difference is, OMB's system was an almost archaic—is an almost archaic system of data processing, and it needed to make a transition to be able to do things in real time, on spreadsheets, with the kind of alacrity that a whiz kid with a computer in 2008 could do. It wouldn't be a hundred percent perfect, because it would miss some of the interactions that the big mainframe could pick up, but it was close enough to keep the process moving and then check it. I think that had I stayed at OMB longer, that was the top of my priority list, to make sure I left OMB with the capacity to play that kind of role with new technology to be as agile as I thought it needed to be.
**Lew:** I'm going to skip over the appropriations negotiations in 2011 to the grand bargain. When we went into the grand-bargain negotiations, the OMB staff was able to do for me everything that it was able to do in the 1990s. I remember there was a process that got set up that was cochaired by Vice President Biden and House majority leader Eric Cantor. You know, strange bedfellows, but they actually developed a warmth and friendship, as I did with Eric Cantor. President Obama never did with Eric Cantor. They were always very much bristly with each other. But the way I developed that relationship with Eric Cantor was—the way the Biden/Cantor process worked was, I was going to brief the group, as OMB director, on all the options for ways to fill a bucket of what we called other mandatory savings: not Medicare, not Medicaid, not Social Security; everything else. And we went through hundreds of items. I think Cantor saw pretty quickly that I was straight. I mean, he had smart people working for him; they never had to say, “That's not correct.” And he developed a confidence that whatever my point of view was, I was going to lay the facts out honestly. Well, it's a lot of power when OMB gives you the ability to play that role in a room.
texts.61:
**Lew:** We actually assembled a list of several hundred billion dollars of things that Cantor and Biden could agree on, and there was no grand bargain, but as you go forward and look at all the little deals that got done after the budget crisis, and when there had to be a relief from the sequestration that was ultimately enacted as part of the budget—what was the name of it? The Budget Enforcement Act? I'm forgetting now what the name of the 2011 sequestration bill was. I should remember it, but I blocked it.
**Lew:**Budget Control Act, the BCA, that's right. The Budget Enforcement Act was Andrews Air Force Base. All of the subsequent deals that, when he was Budget Committee chairman, Paul Ryan and Senator Patty Murray were able to agree to all came out of what we had cobbled together in the months sitting in those rooms together. So it was kind of a glimmer that OMB still had the ability to—I mean, I was the mouthpiece. It's not like I had prior knowledge of more than half of the programs. OMB gives you the ability to speak knowledgeably about things that are new to you. It gives you the ability to sit in a room where you know more than anyone else in the room, even though you didn't know anything about it the day before. That's what was in the notebooks that Dave Stockman had, and in my experience OMB still left me able to do that, even with some loss of edge on some of the—
**Lew:** I mean, the kind of power center, intellectual power center, of OMB was the division that had multiple responsibilities. One was doing cross-government exercises, called BDRs—I struggle to remember what it stands for [budget data requests] —and the other was budget concepts. And the budget-concepts people came through, because the bill that was drafted that put sequestration in place, the Budget Control Act, was written by two guys at my conference table in, basically longhand, because they knew how to do it. They knew how to take the guidance and convert it into a law in unbelievably rapid time, to avoid having a default at the end of that crisis. So I don't want to suggest that OMB had lost its kind of core abilities; there just was a need for a mainframe culture to adapt to the fast pace of policy development in a new world of laptop modelling.
texts.62:
**Lew:** There wasn't great morale at OMB when I got there. I think there was a sense that they were being kind of passed over in some of the first two years of the Obama administration, and my mission, my assignment from President Obama, was: “I know that when you walk in the door, your walking in the door is going to solve that, because people have told me what the morale is going to be when you walk in the door.” He said, “That's one of the reasons I need you to do this.” And I think it worked, in a sense, because I was like one of them. I was the closest thing to being one of them as a political appointee could be. They have to dump on the political people, because it's part of the culture. There's the gray building and there's the red building. The career people work in the red building; the political people work in the gray building. There's always going to be the gray and the red cultures, but I came as close to being accepted by the red-building culture as somebody who lived in the gray building could get, because I'd been there six years, and they knew that I cared deeply about what they did.
**Lew:** When I came back I don't think they knew how hard they were going to work for the next year [laughs] , because no one could imagine going from crisis to crisis, through holidays, literally through every holiday. I remember on Memorial Day and July Fourth being in the kind of peak of battle mode and getting an hour off for the fireworks. [Laughter]
**Q:** So you feel like you left OMB better than—
texts.83:
**Lew:** And the president called me— [laughs] In the eight years of the Obama administration I think I went home sick one day, and it was the day I went home sick, so I was at home with a fever, and the president calls and says, “Jack, I hear you went home sick. I hope you're feeling better, but I want to tell you something: tomorrow Bill Daley is going to be resigning, and I would like to announce you as my new chief of staff. And I said, “Mr. President, I'm honored that you feel that way.” And I said to him, “It's not a job I ever particularly aspired to, but I respect greatly the importance of it. It is the world's biggest pressure cooker, and it's not a decision I can make on my own, particularly not lying in bed with a fever. I've got to call Ruth and talk to my wife. It's a family decision. Let me do that and call you back.”
**Lew:** Why do you want me to be your chief of staff in 2012? You're going to be running for reelection, and it is the most political year of any eight-year presidency, and that's not what I do. I'm not going to be able to help you figure out what you need to do in Pennsylvania or Wisconsin. There are other people who do that for a living.” He said, “That's true, and I've got those people, but they also tell me, and I know they're right, that I'm going to be out there running for president four days a week, and I need a chief of staff who can be my alter ego, who can run this White House and this administration as if I was there, and I trust you to do that.”
**Lew:** So it was a little overwhelming, but—and, as I say, my wife is a true patriot. Her response was, “You can't say no, but you'd better make it a promise to me that you're going to go to the gym every day, because I need you at the end of this.” [Laughter]
**Q:** Did you keep that promise?
texts.84:
**Lew:** I did. Not every day, but certainly I started swimming four or five days a week, and I still do today, and now she thinks I'm a bit of a nut about being disciplined about it. “Actually,” I said, “you're the one who got me started.” [Laughter]
**Q:** When you first stepped into that role, were there things about the process or the structure that you changed?
**Lew:** So, you know, he made the commitment to me that there would be no decision of any consequence that I wasn't fully aware of and have a chance to advise on. There'd be no process that I didn't see, and I'd get to run the White House the way I would. He said, “I know how you deal with people. I know how you bring people together and consult people. You do it the way I would do it. I'm totally comfortable letting you kind of—” There were a few people—he didn't want to have turnover that was unnecessary, and I'm not a “new brush sweeps clean” kind of guy. Some people are. They come in and they say, “I want all my own people.” But when I went to OMB, I kept people who were there before me. When I later went to Treasury, I kept people who were there before me. I always tried to have continuity and have a transition happen gradually, not just say, “Well, I'm the new boss. Thanks for your service.” So that wasn't a big deal to me.
texts.85:
**Lew:** I mean, the challenge in an election year is, there's less of the president's time, so the chief of staff is much more the last stop than in a normal year. When the president is down the hall and if you need to you walk down, you call a meeting—we didn't have that much of his time as we did before or after. So the challenge was to make sure that in all of the decisions we were making, he knew what the views, if they were differing views, were, and could decide if he needed to fit time in to hear it directly. And I needed people to know that their views were going to him, because the whole system would have broken down. I mean, Bill Daley, who preceded me, had a bit of a reputation for being secretive. I think I have the reputation of being a little bit more transparent, so that helps. But it was a dicey situation, because people were used to being able to sit around a table, or in his office around the couches, and kind of offer their own two cents, and that wasn't going to be on every issue, certainly not with the frequency that it otherwise would be.
**Lew:** I pulled the senior staff together in my office, and I made clear I wasn't a “new brush sweeps clean” kind of guy; I wasn't looking to push people out of their roles, and everybody knew me, and I knew everybody, so this doesn't have to be a violent transition. And I said, “Look, I'll make you a commitment: if there's ever disagreements around this table, my chief of staff table, he will know the different points of view, whether he's here and can hear it or not. But you need to make a commitment to me that if you have a differing view, we hear it at this table. There can't be things going to him that don't come through this process. It won't work that way.” My last day as chief of staff, he said to me, “I think I kept my promise. I don't think there was a single decision that didn't go through your office, of any consequence.” It's not that he didn't have social conversations with people. It's not—but he would send everybody back.
texts.86:
**Lew:** There were times when I had to call people on it, where particularly people who had the ability to reach him directly sometimes wanted to keep their own counsel at the table, and on the toughest issue I would go around the room and I'd say, “If I didn't hear from you here, there's no reclama. You don't get to go and make another case. So do you have a view? Do you have a view? Do you have a view?” I just went around the table, and I—and there were some pretty big decisions, like DACA, the Deferred Action for Children, which, we're sitting here on a day when the Supreme Court is hearing oral arguments on whether or not the decision to reverse it was lawful, it was a hard issue to work through, probably the biggest policy issue of my year as chief of staff. We weren't making that much new policy in an election year, but DACA was a big deal.
**Lew:** In the first two years, first three years, the combination of legal analysis and agency views produced a null set in terms of what you could do administratively. The president asked Kathy Ruemmler, who was White House counsel, and me, as chief of staff, to—if we could—not even look at the work that was done before us. He said, “I want you to start from scratch. Things don't always stay the same. Some options change. I want to do something on this.” And it wasn't like I didn't agree with him. One of the issues I've been passionate about in my career has been immigration. I worked on immigration reform in the '80s. I worked on it in the '90s. So it's not like I was in any way disagreeing with him, but it was a pretty daunting assignment when you knew the White House counsel and the Department of Homeland Security and the Justice Department had done this and come up with nothing.
texts.87: **Lew:** So Kathy and I started from scratch, and we worked with the policy teams. We worked with the Department of Homeland Security. And we said, “What if we take a whole different approach, and we just look at what can you do through prosecutorial discretion?” Because you have broad latitude on prosecutorial discretion. Not every crime is prosecuted equally. You don't have to put resources into everything equally. You can't say it's legal, but can you create a space where you can give people at least some temporary protection so that they can get on with their lives? And the interesting thing is, there was a lawful way—in my view; the Supreme Court will maybe decide—to do that. And let's remember the stakes: we didn't know if it was five hundred thousand or a million children who would be affected. These are children who came to this country, grew up here. They didn't cross the border of their own volition; they might have been babies. They went to school here. They served in our armed forces. They were going to our colleges. They were people who, in every way, thought of themselves as Americans, but they had this ambiguity about their status that was a cloud over their ability to get on with their lives. And in order for an approach that involves the kind of discretion that we're talking about here to work, you need the cooperation of the agency that's the enforcement agency. You can't make it happen if there's not a buy-in.

**Lew:** And, you know, he never said another nasty word about me after that, but he didn't vote for me, because he'd already said he wasn't going to vote for me. I think he respected that—I mean, I told him, “I didn't grow up rich like you think I did. I grew up with holes in my shoes. I've worked every day since I was seventeen years old and had, early in my life, responsibilities to support disabled relatives. So don't tell me I don't understand how people who are struggling live. Just don't tell me that. Yes, you didn't like that I worked at Citi for a couple years. I get it. But that doesn't mean you know who I am.”
**Lew:** The exchange at the hearing that, I think, cemented for him that I was “one of them” was over the causes of the financial crisis, where he was just wrong. He said the repeal of Glass-Steagall caused the financial crisis. I said, “Senator, we can debate what the cause of the financial crisis was, but the institutions that failed, that triggered the financial crisis, were doing the same thing they did before Glass-Steagall was repealed. They lived on one side of the line. Lehman [Brothers] was Lehman; Bear [Stearns] was Bear.” And I said there may have been a lot of things that should have been done differently, but it's just not accurate that it was the repeal of Glass-Steagall that caused it, and he took from that exchange that I was being an apologist for the banks. So that was his view of me. It never got any more sophisticated than that. We never really dealt with each other very much after that.
**Q:** You've said before that you spent some time at the Treasury winding down TARP.
**Lew:** Yeah.
**Q:** What did you mean by that?
texts.127:
**Lew:** I got to Treasury in 2013. We were out of the recession. Financial institutions were anxious to pay back TARP and to get out from under quasi-receivership. Institutions like General Motors that had to come and have me approve their compensation plans were anxious to get back to business as usual where they got to do what they wanted on their compensation plans. So we had to have an orderly process of exiting from TARP. It was in no one's interest to extend it. And the question was, do you try to market-time to sell GM stock when the price is good. We did what I would advise somebody to do in the private sector: you have a plan, you execute it, and you don't try to market-time it, and you get out in an orderly way, and on average you'll do okay. I mean, you could easily make a big mistake doing it the other way.
**Lew:** We ended up recovering more than was spent on TARP in repayment, and there were some assets that were valued higher, others that were valued lower, but in the end, if you just look at TARP as, “Did the taxpayers pay for the bailout?” No. It was repaid. Now, that's only half the equation. You look at the damage done to the economy vast damage done to the economy. And how do you measure that? How do you repay for that? I think the political anger that we're still living with is flowing from the fact that it didn't really matter to people that TARP was repaid; it was that the people who caused the crisis got back on their feet, and we didn't. It was that the people who did something wrong didn't go to jail. It was what Tim used to call the desire for Old Testament judgment. It's not my kind of language, but he used to call it that.
texts.128:
**Lew:** The irony is, when I was at OMB, money was not the issue in looking for criminal violations. When I was chief of staff, money was not the issue, and when I was at Treasury money was—the Justice Department had as much resources as it needed. They never found the criminal case to prosecute. And I'm proud to say that our view of the executive branch was you only prosecute when there are crimes, not to make a political statement. You don't put somebody's head on a pike because you want to win a political battle. And I would say of the issues that the president was frustrated over, he saw the schism in the country that was coming from the desire for a greater sense that people who did something wrong needed to pay for it. And it wasn't even in terms of his own politics. I mean, I don't think he thought it was going to be an issue for his politics. He was worried that it was going to undermine confidence in institutions the way it turns out to have. I think had it been like Enron, where there was somebody who could be indicted and pay a price, it probably would have been better for the country.
**Lew:** On the other hand, I'm proud that we didn't just try to indict somebody to make that point, even if we thought it was the right thing in terms of the kind of well-being of democracy. I mean, obviously I'm sitting here in 2020 saying that at a time where there's all kinds of questions about how the lines between Justice Department decision-making and political calculation are very problematic. I remember sitting in a car with the president when the head of state of a very close ally called and said if a certain prosecution goes forward, it could cause a national crisis, economic crisis, damage our relations. And the president said, “Look, our countries are dear friends. We're dear friends. I don't tell the Justice Department what crimes to go after, or what not to go after.”
**Lew:** So this was in a class of frustrating outcomes where we're now in over ten years of uninterrupted economic growth, uninterrupted job growth, people's 401[k]s, IRAs [individual retirement accounts] more than fully restored. There's a lot of ways you can say the recovery was slow but successful. You look at the political and social landscape, and the damage is deep, and I worry about that.
texts.129:
**Q:** We'd like to pivot to some of the foreign policy issues you confronted at Treasury, the first of which being China. In 2006, the Bush administration had created the Strategic Economic Dialogue [SED] . In 2009 the Obama administration stood up the Strategic and Economic Dialogue. Was there significance in that name change?
**Lew:** Well, I must say there is significance. I didn't understand at the time, sitting in the State Department, how symbolic, how much energy would go into thinking about the meaning of it. It seemed obvious to us at the State Department in the first year that the issues between the US and China surely were economic, but they were as much strategic, and we didn't have great mil-mil dialogues between our military and the PLA [People's Liberation Army] . We didn't have the level of connectivity between the State Department and State Council and Foreign Ministry that we should have on hard issues, new issues like cyber, and were not, strictly speaking, economic. I mean, they had economic and strategic components. So the idea was to broaden it, and make it include both, and have two tracks, and have the relationships on both sides evolve.
**Lew:** Treasury wasn't so crazy about the idea, and it's interesting: in the years since, my good friend Hank Paulson continues to talk about the SED, and thinks it was a mistake to expand it to include the strategic issues. And there was some jockeying at the beginning of how many State Department people would be there, and [laughs] it had sometimes comical but classic Washington turf aspects to it. I actually think the way it went forward was quite good. I played a small role in the first one where I was the counterpart on development issues to the Chinese representatives. When I was at OMB and chief of staff, I came in on an issue here, an issue there, but as Treasury secretary I owned the Strategic and Economic Dialogue. And I went into it with some background, but it was the case where I had to get to know a whole new cast of characters. My counterpart was somebody that I met for the first time when we were both named special representative of our respective leaders, and I ended up quickly forging a very good working relationship with him.
texts.207:
**Lew:** Now, some of us may have thought it would have still made sense, while others were happy to leave it behind. That's a separate issue. It's not like everyone, even in the administration, was of one view. Even individuals had—I know I had competing views in my own mind. I think the president had some competing views in his own mind. But once you know you can't do it, you don't spend a lot of your energy trying.
**Q:** I hadn't known much of that. Thanks. Thanks for that. I mentioned I wanted to return to the international global community—and I do—to ask you about Cuba, which I haven't yet had a chance to ask you about over our sessions. And maybe I'll start here. In September of 2015, the Treasury Department joined the Department of Commerce in taking measures to try to normalize relations between the US and Cuba. At the time, you said that action “underscored the administration's commitment to promote successful change for the Cuban people.” What were the aims of the actions the administration took, especially at Treasury, towards Cuba in 2015?
**Lew:** So, there had been a fifty-year economic embargo on Cuba that included all kinds of sanctions that were Treasury-enforced sanctions on dealing with Cuba. The sequence of events—it didn't originate at Treasury. There was a very secret and quiet negotiation driven out of the National Security Council. Ben Rhodes was very much a leader in the effort to work through a way of dealing with Cuba directly on these issues.
**Lew:** When Treasury, which was one of the—I think we were the first non–White House agency that was read into the conversation. They may have been surprised that we were enthusiastically for it, because the Cuba sanctions were viewed as entirely ineffective, harming US economically, and probably setting back the efforts of making things better in Cuba. So there was not a feeling in Treasury that it was a well-designed—even though it was fifty years old—that it was a well-designed, effective set of tools. The political issues surrounding relaxing sanctions on Cuba were much more difficult than the policy and intellectual issues behind the sanctions structure.
texts.208:
**Lew:** Where we got involved was lifting specific sanctions. And I remember going through them with our team from the office at Treasury that deals with sanctions, OFAC, item by item. We were careful to try and do the things that would most encourage people-to-people contact, which had, for a long time, been seen as increasing the likelihood of change in Cuba; helping the Cuban people, who were suffering under economic sanctions that weren't leading to the political aim of sanctions, changing the sovereign policy. The government was not responding to the fact that for decades, it was hurting the Cuban economy. But the Cuban people were hurting.
**Lew:** But we didn't want to be funding the government. We didn't want to give the government the ability to commandeer the benefits of all of the relaxation. And there's no perfect solution, because governments have taxing authority, and it's hard to say that if business increases, and government revenues go in on a normal basis, then you're not helping the larger government. But we tried to avoid the things that would provide lopsided benefit to the government, as opposed to the rank and file. And some of the issues got to things like baseball players [laughs] and things that—where it was very easy to see how it would not be the intended beneficiaries who got the benefit.
**Q:** You, of course, served in the Department of State during the president's first year in office. In 2016, you talked to the reporters a bit about sanctions in a few interviews, and you noted that they were a powerful tool but they shouldn't be used “frivolously.” You also said that policy makers should be as thoughtful about the use of sanctions as they are about the use of military force. I wanted to ask: In that time between 2009 and 2016, how had your view of sanctions evolved, and had your views of sanctions been shaped by your involvement in modifying sanctions against Cuba?
texts.209:
**Lew:** You know, my knowledge of sanctions policy grew quite dramatically in the period from '09 to '17. I worked on some of these sanctions issues from the State Department. And I'll give you an example. This wasn't a Treasury authority, but it's very much the same kind of calculus. I was at the State Department when the Iran sanctions on oil were being negotiated with Congress. This was '09. Congress, including some members of Congress I was very close to, wanted to take the toughest position they could possibly take. And we were pretty confident that if that was the outcome, we wouldn't get the international cooperation that you would need for a sanctions regime to be effective, for countries like Russia and China to participate and not circumvent the sanctions.
**Lew:** We ended up negotiating with Congress to get the flexibility so that you could have, in terms of oil sanctions, variable degrees of reduction, country by country. So if you have a country whose economy would grind to a halt if you shut off all oil imports, they wouldn't have to reduce consumption as much as a country that had very little Iranian oil. And we ended up coming out of it with the lineup that led to the P5+1 talks with Iran and produced the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. China and Russia were very much part of that process. They wouldn't have been if we had done the toughest thing.
**Lew:** So in designing the most effective sanctions regime—and in the things that I said in 2016, I very much spoke to this issue—the purpose of a sanction regime is not just to cause pain to another country; it's to change the policy of another sovereign, to bring the vectors of pressure to bear to accomplish a diplomatic goal. And we did that with Iran by doing it in a way that some might have said wasn't as tough, because it's not always as obvious as, the more severe sanction is going to be more effective.
texts.210:
**Lew:** Something that I learned from '09 through the time I was at Treasury was, war weariness was putting more and more pressure on economic sanctions, because the credibility of threatening to use US force was just in a different place after Iraq and Afghanistan than before. There was just a general sense that the stakes of the US getting involved militarily on the ground had changed. They were not zero, but the bar was higher. The number of circumstances that the US wants to project its influence in doesn't go down when your likelihood or willingness to use force is somewhat lower. Economic tools were a way to use our influence to try to achieve change.
**Lew:** I actually don't think that's a bad thing. I think if you can achieve your change with economic tools instead of putting lives on the line, the world is a better place. But it means you can't do it frivolously, and you can't do it symbolically; because you use those economic tools, you're hurting people. I mean, see Cuba. The Cuban people were poor. The people of North Korea are more poor. The people of Iran were more poor. If it's accomplishing a purpose, you do it in a way that you try to make clear that you don't want to hurt people, but you want the government to change its policy. In a situation where there's no diplomatic strategy that can work, where all it is is hurting people, I think you have to be careful. It may make you feel like you've done something that's moral, but if you actually take it apart, you've caused collateral damage to people who have no ability to change the policy and done nothing to affect the policy-making calculus.
**Lew:** The remarks I gave were actually that it's important to strengthen the tools, not to say don't use them, and, candidly, to make sure that they're there twenty-five, thirty years from now, and they don't get overused and create a flight from the dollar to get away from US pressure—which is not anytime soon, but it's a risk you have to worry about.

'Melograno' is a compelling exploration of the inner turmoil a young teenage boy faces during a weekend trip to meet his estranged father's new girlfriend. Against the picturesque backdrop of the Australian countryside, the film delves into the pervasive issues of misogyny and toxic masculinity, both deeply rooted in society. As the story unfolds, we follow the young protagonist's journey, a poignant coming-of-age tale that strikes a chord with anyone who has ever felt pressured to conform to gender norms and expectations. In his case, these expectations revolve around embracing a hyper-sexualized and performative version of masculinity passed down through generations. The heart of the film lies in the young boy's internal struggle. He grapples with a conflicting desire to forge his identity and assert his individuality while facing the overwhelming weight of societal conformity. 'Melograno' is a window into the emotional complexities of this journey, painting a vivid portrait of his inner conflict. The film's narrative serves as a catalyst for introspection and conversation.
